Temperature is important because it affects how fast your fish\'s metabolism runs. Steady temperature readings matter more than an exact value.
Keep the aquarium out of direct sunlight and away from vents and windows.
Do not change the heater\'s heat output while readings are steady.
Make sure the water temperature of the new water matches the aquarium\'s temperature before a water change.
Compare the aquarium heater\'s heat output against the reading and adjust it a little at a time.
Make sure your aquarium filter or pump is running. If not, the top and the bottom of the aquarium can end up at different temperatures.
Check if sunlight is hitting the aquarium or if a heat vent is blowing nearby.
Too warm? Unplug the heater and point the filter outlet to the surface to cool it down.
Too cold? Check that the heater is turned on and working, then turn its heat output up slowly.
Either way, change the temperature slowly. A fast temperature swing is worse for fish health than the wrong temperature.
Check that the hub is plugged in and the sensor cable is pushed all the way into its port.
Make sure the sensor is under water and its cable is not squeezed behind the aquarium.
If the hub has power but the sensor still sends nothing, pair it again from the app\'s pairing screen.
In case of persistent issues, see Troubleshooting Guide (Settings \u2192 Troubleshooting Guide) or contact customer support (Settings \u2192 Contact & Support) for further assistance.
pH tells you how acidic or basic your water is. It moves up and down a little every day on its own, so a steady reading matters more than an exact value.
Do not try to fix the current pH with pH chemicals. Aquatic creatures handle a steady pH much better than a perfect pH reading.
Keep changing part of the aquarium water regularly. That is what keeps pH from drifting.
Calibrate the pH sensor every few months. An old sensor can slowly start reading incorrectly.
Check the reading with a pH test kit before you change anything.
Change about a quarter of the water and look again in a few hours.
Take out leftover fish food and dead leaves, and make sure the aquarium filter is not clogged.
Check the reading with a pH test kit before you add anything to the water and make sure the filter is working properly.
Change about a quarter of the water at a time. One big pH change is harder on the fish than the bad reading.
A high pH reading may point to high ammonia levels. In case of a high pH reading, test the ammonia level.
Make sure that the sensor is submeregd in water and its plug is pushed into the hub.
Look at the glass tip of the sensor for cracks or for a dried out end.
Once it works again, calibrate it from Settings \u2192 Sensor Calibration. Buy pH buffer solutions for accurate calibration.
In case of persistent issues, see Troubleshooting Guide (Settings \u2192 Troubleshooting Guide) or contact customer support (Settings \u2192 Contact & Support) for further assistance.
Dissolved solids tells you about everything dissolved in your water, like minerals, salts and fish waste. It slowly goes up between water changes and drops right after one.
Look at the reading right after a water change. That number is what normal looks like for your aquarium!
Watch how the number moves over a few days. One reading on its own does not say much.
Fill up evaporated water in the aquarium tank with filtered water. Tap water leaves more minerals behind every time.
If the TDS reading is high, change about a quarter of the water and look again tomorrow.
If the TDS reading is low, add minerals slowly over a few days.
Feed your aquatic creatures less, feed only what your fish finishes in about two minutes, and clean the gravel.
Change about a quarter of the aquarium water now, and again each day until the TDS reading becomes normal.
Match the new water to the aquarium\'s temperature and treat it for chlorine first.
Make sure the aquarium filter is not clogged, and clean out any rotting food or plants.
Check that the sensor is under water and its plug is pushed into the hub.
Dry the sensor\'s metal pins and plug it back in. Rust on them is the usual reason.
Once it works again, calibrate it from Settings → Sensor Calibration.
In case of persistent issues, see Troubleshooting Guide (Settings \u2192 Troubleshooting Guide) or contact customer support (Settings \u2192 Contact & Support) for further assistance.

Water Level is a simple water detector. It only alerts you if the water drops below the spot where it sits, not how deep the water is. Attach the water level sensor at the appropriate height of your aquarium\'s water level!
Your aquarium\'s water level is currently fine :)
The water has dropped below the sensor. Your aquarium needs a water refill!!!
There is still water at the sensor\'s height, but your thresholds mark this as a warning.
Make sure that the sensor is attached flat against the outside of the glass on your desired water level height. It reads through the glass, so it has to sit tight against it.
Keep the lid on. A covered aquarium loses much less water!
Fill up evaporated water with tap water treated for chlorine, at the same temperature as the aquarium.
Look at the aquarium and fill it up if the water has dropped close to the sensor.
Wipe the outside of the glass around the sensor. Water drips running down the aquarium surface can confuse the reading.
Make sure the sensor is attached flat against the outside of the glass, with nothing between the two.
Make sure the sensor is attached flat against the outside of the aquarium glass, with nothing between the two.
Refill the aquarium immediately with tap water treated for chlorine, at the same temperature as the aquarium.
Once the water is refilled, check that the filter is under water and running again.
Check that the hub is plugged in and the sensor cable is pushed all the way into its port.
Make sure the sensor is attached flat to the outside of the glass, with nothing between the two.
If the hub has power but still sends no reading, pair it again from the pairing screen.

Correction quality gives you a quick sense of the calibration result. The percentage compares the gap between the sensor readings collected during calibration and the set operating point with the width of the normal range. Lower is better. If it is high, recalibrate in a stable environment. If it remains high, replace the sensor.
Partly cloudy: adjustment up to 10 percent

Prepare a container of water at a value inside this aquarium\'s normal range, and confirm it with a reference instrument you trust. Pick a value the tank actually sits at: the correction is most accurate where it is measured.

Enter the value you brought the water to, keep everything still, and tap Calibrate. AquaSense averages every raw reading it receives over the next %1$d seconds and stores the difference as this sensor\'s correction.
I am ready to hold the probe and water still
A single correction is exact where it was taken and drifts either side of it, so calibrate at a value your aquarium normally holds.

1. Empty or lower the tank water below the sensor trigger point.
2. Confirm the app shows a low / empty reading.
3. Raise the water to the normal fill line.
4. Confirm the app shows a full / normal reading.
5. Adjust the sensor position if the trigger point is off.

1. Place the sensor in a verified ice-water bath (0 °C / 32 °F).
2. Wait 60 seconds for the reading to stabilise.
3. Optionally repeat with a warm reference (e.g. 40 °C / 104 °F).
4. Note any offset and adjust in your controller if needed.

1. Rinse the probe with distilled water.
2. Submerge in a 0 ppm (DI) solution and wait 30 seconds for a near-zero reading.
3. Rinse, then submerge in a known TDS calibration solution (e.g. 342 ppm or 1000 ppm).
4. Wait for the reading to match the solution value, then rinse before returning to the tank.

1. Rinse the probe with distilled water.
2. Submerge in pH 7 buffer solution for 60 seconds.
3. Rinse again, then submerge in pH 4 (or pH 10) buffer for 60 seconds.
4. Rinse thoroughly. The probe is ready.

Set up your smart aquarium monitor in three simple steps :)
Name your aquarium and choose the template its safe ranges come from or create a custom one.
Mount the hub and attach the four AquaSense sensors to your aquarium.
Find your hub over Bluetooth and hand it your Wi-Fi credentials so it can start sending you aquarium readings!

The structure of a set-up aquarium: the hub hangs on the aquarium rim edge by its hooks. The waterline marks the level it watches. Three probes are submerged in the water, and the water level sensor is stuck to the outside of the glass.
Attach the hardware hub to your aquarium before pairing. The hub needs to be set up and powered up before progressing to the next step.
Hang the hub on the rim of your aquarium within reach of a power outlet. Keep the enclosure itself out of the water.
Put the three sensor probes in the water
Submerge the temperature, pH and dissolved solids probes below the water surface, away from the filter outlet and gravel.

Attach the water level sensor to the outside of the aquarium wall, at the lowest level you will allow the water to drop down to. The water level sensor senses through the glass, so it never goes in the water, and it reports Low the moment the water surface drops past it.
Plug the hub in and wait for its light to start blinking. A blinking light means it is ready to be paired to the app on the next step.
\"%1$s\" is ready to monitor. Head to your dashboard to watch its live readings.

TDS sensor range (1-1600 ppm) is below saltwater levels, so it is disabled for saltwater aquariums. Marine salinity can be measured with a refractometer or a salinity sensor instead.

Why is Dissolved Solids not here?
Why is Water Level not here?

The hub\’s water level sensor is a capacitive detector mounted on the outside of the aquarium tank. It only detects whether water is at the level of its position, alerting "Normal" when it detects water and "Critical" water drops below its level. So, there is no threshold range to set for this sensor. To adjust the water level trigger, physically move the sensor up or down.
